title: Kenyan Smokie Pasua
community: Popular across urban Kenya — a Nairobi street food icon
author: Mama Wanjiru
desc: Smokie Pasua is Nairobi's most iconic street food — a smoked sausage (smokie) split open (pasua means 'to split' in Swahili), filled with kachumbari, pili pili sauce, and sometimes bhajia or chips, then eaten on the go. A Nairobi institution.
longDesc: 'Pasua' — split it open. That is the entire concept and the genius of smokie pasua. A smoked sausage, grilled until hot and slightly charred, is split lengthwise and filled with raw kachumbari — tomatoes, onions, coriander, lemon — and pili pili sauce. The contrast of the hot, smoky sausage with the fresh, acidic kachumbari stuffed inside it is one of the most satisfying flavour combinations in Kenyan street food. At Nairobi bus stops and street corners in the evening, smokie vendors are as much a part of the landscape as the matatus.
steps: Make the kachumbari filling: combine diced tomatoes, onion, chilli, coriander, lemon juice, and salt. Toss and set aside.
Heat a grill or pan over high heat. Add oil.
Grill the smokies for 4—5 minutes, turning, until heated through and slightly charred on the outside.
Remove from heat. Using a sharp knife, cut the smokie lengthwise — split it almost all the way through without cutting completely in half.
Open the smokie like a book.
Spoon kachumbari generously into the split. Add pili pili sauce.
Serve immediately — eat on the go or on a plate.
chefTips: Cut the smokie almost all the way through but keep it hinged — this creates a pocket that holds the filling.
The kachumbari should be fresh and sharp — the acid of the lemon against the smoky sausage is the whole point.
Add bhajia or chips inside for the ultimate Nairobi street food experience.
commonMistakes: Cutting the smokie completely in half — it should open like a book, not split into two pieces.
Serving without fresh kachumbari — this is not optional.

faqs.a: A smokie is a smoked beef sausage — pre-cooked during smoking, so it only needs to be heated through before serving. It is widely available in Kenyan supermarkets and butcheries.
Pasua is Swahili for split or cut open. Smokie pasua literally means split smokie — the defining preparation that distinguishes it from a plain grilled smokie.

cookingScience: Smokies are cured and smoked during production — the smoke deposits phenolic compounds on the surface that act as natural preservatives and contribute the distinctive smoky flavour. The final grilling reheats the sausage and creates additional Maillard browning on the casing.
sustainabilityTips: Buy from local Kenyan sausage makers rather than imported brands where possible.
healthBenefits: Kachumbari adds vitamins from fresh vegetables.
culturalNote: Smokie Pasua is as Nairobi as the matatu — a street food that has become inseparable from the rhythm of the city's evening commute. It is the snack that fuels workers heading home, students leaving campus, and anyone who needs something hot, satisfying, and portable before reaching their destination.
regionalVariations: Smokie pasua with chips inside — the ultimate loaded version.
